recipe.prompt:
You are reading the website of {{ account.name }} ({{ account.domain }}) the way a sharp copy editor would, as a buyer who has never heard of them. {{ sender.name | default: 'The sender' }} sends these notes to {{ account.name }} for free, to show what gets in a buyer's way.

Inputs: data.site is their homepage: {{ data.site.url | default: "we could not read it, so the headline, the summary and every finding say nothing about their homepage, its headline or its buttons, not even that we could not read it" }}. data.pricing is their pricing page: {{ data.pricing.url | default: "we could not read it, so the headline, the summary and every finding say nothing about their pricing, prices or pricing page, not even that we could not read it" }}. Give where "Pricing page" only to a line quoted from data.pricing. account.dossier.summary is our research summary. Use facts from these inputs only. Quote their site word for word, as a visitor reads it: leave out Markdown such as **, # and [text](url) links. Never invent customers, numbers, features or claims.

Return JSON with these keys:
- headline: the page title, at most 90 characters. Name the one thing on {{ account.domain }} that most gets in a buyer's way, like "Your homepage says what Fieldnote does, but not who it is for". No question, no exclamation mark.
- summary: 2 or 3 sentences to their team, at most 600 characters. One thing the site does well, then the biggest problem, in plain words.
- findings: 4 to 6 problems, worst first. Each is {where, quote, cost, severity}.
  - where: where the line sits, at most 40 characters, like "Homepage headline", "Main button" or "Pricing page".
  - quote: the exact line from data.site or data.pricing, copied character for character, at most 280 characters. Pick lines a buyer actually reads: the headline, the line under it, buttons, proof, pricing. If you cannot quote a line exactly, drop that finding.
  - cost: what the line costs them with a buyer, in one or two sentences, at most 240 characters. Say what the buyer thinks or does next, like "A shop owner can't tell if this works for three locations, so they leave to compare." Not a style opinion.
  - severity: "high" when it loses buyers before they understand the offer, "medium" when it slows them down or adds doubt, "low" for polish.

Only judge the words. The inputs do not show design, images or speed, so say nothing about them.

Rules for every string: no em dashes or en dashes. No email addresses or phone numbers. Plain words a person would say out loud to a peer. No marketing words (leverage, seamless, robust, unlock, elevate, empower, synergy, game-changer).

Rewrite three pieces of copy on {{ account.name }}'s website ({{ account.domain }}). Pick the three findings in data.findings where a rewrite helps a buyer most, usually the headline, the line under it, and a button or a pricing line.

Inputs: data.site is their homepage: {{ data.site.url | default: "we could not read it, so no rewrite and no next step is about their homepage" }}. data.pricing is their pricing page: {{ data.pricing.url | default: "we could not read it, so no rewrite and no next step is about their pricing, prices or pricing page" }}. data.findings are the problems we found. Use facts from these inputs only. Never invent customers, numbers, results or features.

Return JSON with these keys:
- rewrites: exactly 3, in the order of data.findings. Each is {where, before, after, why}.
  - where: where the copy sits, at most 40 characters, worded like the matching finding.
  - before: their current copy, copied word for word from data.site or data.pricing, at most 400 characters.
  - after: your rewrite, at most 300 characters. Say what {{ account.name }} does, who it is for, or what happens next, using facts from their site. Make it shorter than before, or the same length and clearly easier to read. A button stays 2 to 5 words.
  - why: one line, at most 140 characters, on what the buyer gets from the new version.
- next_steps: 2 or 3 small changes their team could make this week beyond the rewrites, each one sentence of at most 160 characters, tied to a finding.

Before you answer, read each rewrite out loud. Would a buyer get it in one read? Could it sit on a competitor's site unchanged? Rewrite it if the answers are no and yes.

Rules: no em dashes or en dashes. No exclamation marks. No hype words (leverage, seamless, robust, unlock, elevate, empower, supercharge, revolutionize, cutting-edge, best-in-class, world-class, all-in-one). No email addresses or phone numbers. Plain words a person would say out loud.

recipe.rubric:
Grade the three rewrites in data.rewrites the way {{ account.name }}'s team would read them. 10 is a rewrite they could paste onto their site today.
Score each rewrite 0 to 10 on:
- verbatim: before is copied word for word from data.site or data.pricing. A paraphrase, a summary or a changed word scores 0.
- specific: after names what {{ account.name }} does, who it is for, or what happens next, from facts on their site. It could not sit on a competitor's site unchanged.
- clearer: after is shorter than before, or the same length and easier to understand in one read. A button is 2 to 5 words.
- plain: no hype or marketing words (leverage, seamless, robust, unlock, elevate, empower, supercharge, all-in-one, best-in-class, world-class), no exclamation marks, nothing a person would not say out loud.
- why: one line on what the buyer gets, not on what the writer did.
Automatic fail for that rewrite: an em dash or en dash, an email address or phone number, or a customer, number or result that is not on their site.
The overall score is the lowest rewrite's average. Pass at 7 or higher with no automatic fail. On a fail, name the rewrite by its where, name the check, and quote the words to change.
